query: For multiprincipal-element alloys intended for sustained use in harsh high-temperature environments, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs oxidation resistance and material integrity, and why? Define a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing behavior, the observations predicted relative to a baseline, the range over which the hypothesis should hold, relevant supporting evidence, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Precipitation aging of the SLM Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy introduces dual nanoprecipitates (Ni/Ti-enriched L12 and Al/Ti-enriched L21) that deplete Cr locally and create additional matrix–precipitate interfaces. This Cr depletion delays the formation of a continuous protective Cr2O3 scale and provides short-circuit oxygen diffusion paths, thereby increasing oxidation mass gain at high temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: SLM as-printed Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with a >97%-dense, single-fcc cellular microstructure and a uniform Cr distribution.
generation.intervention: Aging the as-printed alloy at 750°C for 50 hours to induce formation of approximately 25–30 vol% nanoprecipitates (Ni/Ti-enriched L12 and larger Al/Ti-enriched, Cr/Fe-depleted L21 precipitates).
generation.conditions: Isothermal oxidation of polished 7.5 × 7.5 × 3 mm samples at 600, 750, 900, 1050, and 1200°C for durations up to 96 hours with intermittent mass gain and oxide-thickness measurements.
generation.structural_mediator: A duplex-to-trilayer oxide scale develops, consisting of an outer layer of elemental/mixed/spinel oxides, an intermediate continuous Cr-rich oxide (primarily Cr2O3) layer, and an inner discontinuous Al/Ti-rich oxide region. In the aged alloy, the presence of Cr-depleted precipitates and additional matrix–precipitate interfaces interferes with the uniform growth of the protective Cr-rich layer.
generation.mechanism: In the as-printed alloy, uniform Cr distribution promotes early formation of a continuous Cr2O3 barrier that limits inward oxygen diffusion. In contrast, aging-induced precipitates create regions with reduced Cr, delaying the formation of a protective Cr2O3 scale and permitting increased oxygen ingress through defects or along interfaces, particularly at higher temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the as-printed baseline, the precipitation-aged alloy is expected to show higher oxidation mass gain—especially at temperatures above 900°C—due to a delayed and compromised Cr-rich scale formation, while both states maintain similar high-temperature oxide-growth activation energies once a Cr2O3 layer eventually forms.
generation.baseline: SLM as-printed alloy with uniform Cr distribution that enables rapid, continuous formation of a dense Cr2O3 layer, resulting in lower oxidation mass gain.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold over a temperature range of approximately 600–1200°C and exposure times up to 96 hours. Notably, below about 900°C, the Cr-rich scale is sufficiently protective, whereas the mismatch in oxidation behavior becomes more apparent at higher temperatures.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative differences in oxidation kinetics and activation energies between the two states remain uncertain due to variations in precipitate distribution and local oxygen diffusion pathways.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct time-resolved oxidation experiments comparing the as-printed and precipitation-aged alloys under identical conditions (600–1200°C, up to 96h). Utilize measures including mass gain, oxide thickness (via cross-sectional SEM), and phase/elemental analysis (via SEM-EDS, XRD, and Raman spectroscopy) to characterize the evolution and structure of the oxide scales.
measurements: Mass gain curves over time at each temperature
Oxide layer thickness from cross-sectional SEM imaging
Elemental mapping and phase identification from SEM-EDS, XRD, and Raman spectroscopy
Arrhenius activation energy determination from oxide growth rates
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the precipitation-aged alloy does not exhibit a significantly higher oxidation mass gain at higher temperatures (≥900°C) relative to the as-printed alloy, or if similar protective Cr2O3 scales form with no delay or increased oxygen diffusion pathways, the hypothesis will be rejected.
